\chapter{Numbers Eleven to Twenty}
\label{ch:ar-numbers-eleven-to-twenty}

Each section stays independently resumable and preserves the authored prerequisite order.

\section[\ar{أحد} \ar{عشر} — \ar{عشرون}]{\ar{أحد} \ar{عشر}, \ar{عشرون} — plain compounds, then a genuinely different twenty}

\label{lesson:AR-C20-ahada-ashar-ishrun}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Eleven through fifteen build the same simple way every time. Then twenty breaks the pattern completely — it isn't built the way you'd expect at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{أحد} \ar{عشر} – \ar{خمسة} \ar{عشر} — "X and ten"}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{أحد} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{aḥada ʿashar} — "one-ten" (11) \\
\textbf{\ar{اثنا} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{ithnā ʿashar} — "two-ten" (12) \\
\textbf{\ar{ثلاثة} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{thalāthata ʿashar} — "three-ten" (13) \\
\textbf{\ar{أربعة} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{arbaʿata ʿashar} — "four-ten" (14) \\
\textbf{\ar{خمسة} \ar{عشر}} & \emph{khamsata ʿashar} — "five-ten" (15) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one of these is the counting-word (from the AGE and NUM-1-5 lessons) plus \textbf{\ar{عشر}} (\emph{ʿashar}, "\textbf{ten}") — a straightforward additive compound, the same shape you've now seen in Spanish's \emph{once}-\emph{quince} and Latin's \emph{ūndecim}-\emph{quīndecim}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{عشرون} — NOT "two-ten," a genuinely different word}
Here's the honest surprise: \textbf{twenty} is \textbf{not} built from "two" + "ten" the way 11-15 were built. \textbf{\ar{عشرون}} (\emph{ʿishrūn}, "twenty") is its \textbf{own}, distinct word — a special \textbf{plural-like form} built directly on the same "ten" root, \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ش}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ʿ-sh-r}), rather than a compound of \emph{ithnān} ("two") and \emph{ʿashar} ("ten"). That root, \emph{ʿashar}/\emph{ʿishrūn}, is the same Semitic "ten" root behind Hebrew's \textbf{\he{עֶשֶׂר}} (\emph{eser}, "ten") — and, coincidentally, resembles the Indo-European "ten" root that gives English its own \textbf{-teen} suffix, though the two roots are \textbf{not} related: Arabic and English inherited "ten" from two entirely separate language families, so this is a parallel, not a shared borrowing or common ancestor.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "aḥada ʿashar, ithnā ʿashar, thalāthata ʿashar" — 11, 12, 13, "X and ten"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ʿishrūn" — twenty, its OWN word, not "two-ten"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} How are 11-15 built in Arabic? (\textbf{X + ʿashar} — "one-ten," "two-ten," and so on, a plain additive compound.) Is \textbf{\ar{عشرون}} (twenty) built the same way, as "two-ten"? (\textbf{No} — it's a distinct, standalone plural-like form built on the same "ten" root, not a compound of "two" and "ten.") What root does \textbf{ʿashar}/\textbf{ʿishrūn} share with Hebrew? (\textbf{\he{ע}-\he{ש}-\he{ר}}/\textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ش}-\ar{ر}}, the Semitic root for "ten," giving Hebrew's \emph{eser}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
